“In a recent paper.... Luce has called irrigated rice the prime prod- 
uct of South-East Asia, and one of the great discoveries of humanity. The 
rubicon between dry and wet rice he claims was crossed by the advanced 
Mon-Khmer speaking people of Indo-China Peninsula. They pioneed its 
cultivation, in the delta of Red river in Tonking. Their efforts, he thinks 
caused a population explosion. This in turn led to the other delta areas 
and foundation of centres of wet rice cultivation near the mouths of the 
Mekong, the Menam and the Irrawadi. 

... When the Tonking plain was overran by the Vietnamese, the 
majority of the wet rice cultivators living there, went up the Red river to 
Yunnan, then escaping westwards from the cold, high plateau of Central 
Yunnan, they followed the Red river to its source, south of Tali, made 
their way across northern Burma to Khasi in the plain of East Assam 
where they established a new centre. The main body, however, moved 
into the plain of Ganges whence Aryan penetration drove them into the 
hills of Central and Eastern India. Hence their descendants are met with 
today are speakers of the Munda language, and number some four mil- 
lions.” (G.E.Hail, History of South-East Asia, 1994, p.221). 

Kat kum u Luce, ka Jaidbynriew kaba kren ia ka ktien Mon Khmer 
ba ka Jaidbynriew ba kham stad ka la lap nyngkong ka rukom rep 3 ung 
bad rep hali ha ki rud-duriaw kiba ka wah Tonking ka tuid lyngba bad ka 
jingsdang rep kba ha ki sung ka la wallam ia ka jingiar bakhraw ha ka 
jingbunbriew jong ka jaidbynriew ba kren ia ka ktien Mon-Khmer (kaba

ngi hiar pateng). Bad ka rep hali kumjuh ka la phriang ha ki shyntur jong 
ka wah Irrawadi, wah Mekong bad wah Menam. Halor ka jingiaknieh 
khyndew, kawei ka kynhun ka la ieh noh syndon ia la ki shnong bad ka la 
phet sha Yunnan lyngba ka phud wah jong ka Red river, na Yunnan ba la 
khriat palat, ka kynhun ka bud ter ter shaduh ki tlong jong kata ka wah, 
shaphang shathie na ka jaka ba la jer ka Tali, nangta sha Burma bashatei 
shaduh ki pyntha ka mihngi jong ka ri Assam kaba la ju khot mynshuwa 
ka Ri Khasi. Kawei pat ka kynhun ka tur shaphang sepngi sha ki rud ka 
wah Ganges nangta sha ki lum ka pdeng bad ka India mihngi kaba mynta 
ngi tip ia ka kum ka Munda bad kaba ka jingbunbriew ka la jan kot shaduh 
saw million ne.

Ka kot ba la jer “Geological structure of part of the Khasi Hills” 
1 854, u nongthoh, Thomas Oldham, u shem kumne: “a large proportion of

potatoes is annually sent from the hills. For the most part these potatoes 
are purchased in small quantities in each family by Khasi merchants or 
by Bengalese who come up for the purpose and the accumulated store is 
then shipped from Pondua or Chattue (Chatak) to Calcutta. From the hills 
also, Culcutta and other places are principally supplied with pine-apples. 
They grow freely along the lower slopes of the hills, and are of good 
quality. The same plant furnishes the Khasi with the strong and the smooth 
fibre of which his netter pouch is made, and which is usefully applied in a 
thousand other ways.” 

On oranges : “The first fruit is small roundish with rinds, and like 
the variety so well known at Malta under the name of Mandarin orange”. 
About orange plantation : “The orange groves stretch for miles along the 
flat ground just at the base of the hills, and are very well kept, and con- 
stantly renewed. The fruit is the only product of the trees more economised. 
The manufacture of flower water which in the south of Europe is so ex- 
tensively carried on, and which there forms a very considerable profits is 
here unknown”.

“The quality of Khasi coal” Oldham remarked “has been frequently 
spoken of, ... as being greatly superior to the Burdwan ...and as being 
equal in every respect to English coal. The Cherra coal is undoubtedly 
superior to coal from Damoodah valley... and it is equally certain that it is 
equal to some English coals, but is is certainly inferior to others. It is 
quick in action and therefore would generate steam rapidly : It cakes well 
but gives a large amount of smoke, ... As a gas producing coal, it is supe- 
rior to good English coal. But as regards the quantity and quality of its gits 
with proper precautions in burning, it would yield a very passable coke”.

“The attendants came up the hills, armed with swords, bows and 
quivers. The Rajah proceeded to explain the object of the meeting and 
requested the different orators to express their sentiments on the proposi-

opposition immediately... commenced a long harangue in condemnation 
of the measures expressed in a continuous flow of language accompanied 
with much animation of manner and appropriate gesticulation. This was 
replied to by an orator of the Rajah’s party and in this way the ball was 
kept rolling until evening”. The official observed: “I was struck with 
astonishment at the order and decorum which character] cd these debates. 
No shout of exultation or indecent attemps to put down the orator of the 
opposite party was made. On the contrary, every speaker was fairly heard 
out. 1 have often witnessed the debates in St. Stephen's Chapel which is 
British Parliament” but those of the Khasi Parliament appeared to me to 
be conducted with more dignity of manner. 

As it grew dark, the debate not being closed, Mr. Scott rather grew
